analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to share parts, tools, and repair manuals so independent shops and owners can fix devices.
analysis.headline: The Fair Repair Act never received a committee vote or floor vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require makers of digital electronic equipment to sell or provide documentation, parts, and repair tools to independent repair shops and equipment owners on the same terms they give their own authorized repair networks. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules. The bill excludes motor vehicles and medical devices.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of phones, laptops, farm equipment, and other electronics who want to repair what they bought instead of replacing it, and the independent repair shops and technicians who compete with manufacturer-authorized repair networks. Easier access to parts and manuals means cheaper repairs and longer-lasting devices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must make documentation, parts, and tools (including software needed to pair or calibrate new parts) available to independent repair providers and owners on fair and reasonable terms, defined as no worse than the best terms offered to their own authorized repair networks.
For equipment under warranty with a wholesale price of $100 or more, manufacturers must provide what is needed to repair it at an equitable price, based on their actual distribution cost.
Manufacturers must also provide what is needed to bypass and reset electronic security locks during repair, though this can be done through secure data-release systems.
The Federal Trade Commission can enforce the requirements, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents for injunctions, penalties, and restitution.

analysis.who_pays: Original equipment manufacturers — makers of phones, computers, and other digital electronics — give up exclusive control over repair parts, manuals, and diagnostic tools, and lose some of the revenue that comes from steering customers to their own repair services or pushing them to buy replacements. Taxpayers bear the modest cost of FTC enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The bill is carved back substantially before it starts: it does not apply to motor vehicles or motor vehicle equipment, and it does not apply to medical devices, two of the areas where repair restrictions are most debated.

Manufacturers argued in the broader right-to-repair debate that giving outsiders access to security locks and diagnostic software creates safety, security, and intellectual-property risks; the bill responds by protecting trade secrets and allowing secure data-release systems, but does not eliminate the underlying concern.

'Fair and reasonable terms' would require case-by-case judgment and enforcement, so the practical price and availability of parts would depend on FTC and state enforcement rather than being guaranteed outright.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For device owners, the benefits are concrete: cheaper repairs, longer-lasting electronics, and less forced replacement. The main costs fall on manufacturers' repair and replacement revenue, not on consumers. The bill's real weakness is scope — by excluding cars and medical devices, it covers less of the repair-restriction problem than its name suggests — and its reliance on after-the-fact enforcement rather than automatic price rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Consumer Protection subcommittee in June 2021, and no markup, vote, or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Morelle introduced the Fair Repair Act on June 17, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, where it stayed; no further action was taken for the rest of the 117th Congress.
Eleven Democratic members cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any hearing in the House, and no Senate companion action appears in its history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics and equipment manufacturers keep their exclusive control over parts, repair tools, and service information, and the authorized-repair economics built on that control are unchanged. Consumers keep paying manufacturer-set repair prices and replacing devices they could have fixed.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters (the sponsor and 11 cosponsors) were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the committee that declined to act was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Consumer electronics and digital equipment manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would force makers of phones, laptops, and other digital equipment to sell parts, tools, and manuals to independent shops and owners on equal terms, cutting into their repair and replacement revenue. Companies like Apple have fought right-to-repair rules for exactly this reason.

The bill's core beneficiaries outside consumers: independent repair providers would gain legal access on equal terms to the parts, documentation, and diagnostic tools now reserved for manufacturer-authorized networks.

industries.industry: Motor vehicle and medical device manufacturers
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes motor vehicles and medical devices, so manufacturers in those sectors keep their existing repair-restriction arrangements untouched.
